_note: English glossary for the atom library. Keys are atom ids from atoms/index.json; values are [English name, one-line definition]. Read by tools/build_site.py.

zhexuan.1: First, grant that what the reader feels right now is legitimate.
zhexuan.2: Don't answer the question asked; turn a personal problem into one about the era or the standard.
zhexuan.3: Where doubt runs hottest, place one precise, close-to-home number.
zhexuan.4: Give an abstract claim body heat with one specific person, image or detail.
zhexuan.5: Break a vague target of criticism into types, steps or stages you can count.
zhexuan.6: Rewrite a misused concept as "not A, but B".
zhexuan.7: Alternate historical anchors with present cases so the conclusion has depth in time.
zhexuan.8: Aim criticism at the concrete level of execution; keep the abstract principle protected.
zhexuan.9: End on three parallel lines or a matched pair: a stance the reader can carry away.
zhexuan.10: Press the argument into one line that holds outside its context.
zhexuan.11: Topic choice: collective feeling building up, times a moment no authority has answered.
zhexuan.12: Treat readers as people thinking it through with you, not people being taught.
jinyong.1: On a character's first appearance, pin them down with one action, one oddity, one line.
jinyong.2: Cut a fight into shots: who is where, what move, why, and what follows.
jinyong.3: Give moves names with a lineage tied to the character, and name them only at key moments.
jinyong.4: Show early that a character is withholding something, and keep it withheld.
jinyong.5: At the height of conflict, turn up the truth and rearrange everyone's position.
jinyong.6: Several parties share a scene; a few strokes each show their separate calculations.
jinyong.7: Make a character choose between two right things, and pay for it.
jinyong.8: Ground the story in a real reign or war, with private feuds under the larger tide.
jinyong.9: Write chapter titles as a matched couplet, each half pointing to one plot turn.
jinyong.10: Everyone speaks differently; hide the names and you still know who is talking.
lijuan.1: The narrator plays the one who doesn't understand, seeing things as if for the first time.
lijuan.2: Write out the steps, quantities and feel of a small task one by one; never summarize.
lijuan.3: Write sky, snow and grass in nouns and verbs, exact in color and shape, with no big words.
lijuan.4: Write yourself clumsy, timid or embarrassed, and laugh before the reader does.
lijuan.5: Sketch what family members do and say without judging; let them be funny, with tenderness inside.
lijuan.6: State an obvious exaggeration with honest numbers and a serious tone.
lijuan.7: Talk to animals, plants and weather as neighbors with tempers of their own.
lijuan.8: Mid-scene, widen the view to the whole town or sky, and people suddenly shrink.
lijuan.9: When feeling peaks, press it into one ordinary sentence, then return to chores.
lijuan.10: Don't sum up or elevate; stop on an action, a line, or an image.
luxun.1: Start from something too small for anyone to have thought of writing about.
luxun.2: Criticize in the voice of praise, following the logic until the absurdity shows.
luxun.3: Press a long-circled phenomenon into one cold judgment of what it is.
luxun.4: Name a kind of person or mindset so that everyone recognizes it from then on.
luxun.5: State the other side fully, even better than they do, then take it apart.
luxun.6: Hold an old book or old event up to today: new clothes, same bones.
luxun.7: Sketch "a person like this" in a few strokes, naming no one, so everyone fits.
luxun.8: Turn the knife on yourself too, admitting you belong to the group under criticism.
luxun.9: Feeling stays unspoken, and the coldest line is the last one.
luxun.10: No elevation, no solution: leave a cold line or a question.
mao.1: The first sentence states the problem or the thesis, with no detour.
mao.2: Sort the subject into classes by one criterion; give the facts and stance for each.
mao.3: Number problems or remedies first, second, third; each opens with a short line.
mao.4: Make abstract reasoning visible with common sayings and everyday things.
mao.5: Grant that a matter has two sides, then say which one is principal.
mao.6: Sketch a wrong way of working, give it a memorable name, describe the conduct, name no one.
mao.7: Set a benchmark with a specific person or deed: this is how it should be done.
mao.8: Voice the objection first, grant what is reasonable in it, then answer.
mao.9: Run several short sentences of the same shape, each pushing the next.
mao.10: End with one concrete thing to do, in the tone of a suggestion.
guanfang.1: In the first paragraph, place the issue on the national and historical map and give the overall judgment.
guanfang.2: Mark where "now" sits with dates or stages, explaining why it is said now.
guanfang.3: Draw a path from reliable history to show today's choice has roots.
guanfang.4: Set sourced figures beside judgments so the numbers give them weight.
guanfang.5: Bring a grand theme down to one person, one village, one workshop.
guanfang.6: Compress points into sets of four-character phrases for a formal cadence.
guanfang.7: Close a paragraph or section with a symmetrical, complementary pair of sentences.
guanfang.8: Three to five same-shaped sentences climb from small to large, from person to nation.
guanfang.9: Admit the difficulty or doubt openly, then answer from a higher level.
guanfang.10: End on "we" and "action": confidence and direction drawn from what came before.
standup.1: Open on a small detail everyone has lived through but no one has said.
standup.2: One line builds an expectation; the next overturns it in as few words as possible.
standup.3: Flip the whole logic of a bit, swapping identity or cause and effect.
standup.4: Two normal examples set a pattern; the third keeps the shape and goes wrong.
standup.5: Put yourself in the spot to be laughed at first.
standup.6: Accept a small premise and follow it, straight-faced, into the absurd.
standup.7: Don't describe it; perform the character, the object, the inner voice.
standup.8: Bring back an earlier joke in a new context so it lands again.
standup.9: Compare with a completely unrelated field; the more precise, the funnier.
standup.10: Keep the punchline under ten characters, end on a noun or verb, then stop.
sushi.1: One sentence gives time, place and occasion, then straight in.
sushi.2: Admit freely to being idle and useless, and treat it as the right to see good things.
sushi.3: Describe a bad situation honestly first, then find something in it to enjoy.
sushi.4: Let a guest voice the common gloom, and answer it at ease.
sushi.5: Look at the same thing on a different scale, and the worry loosens by itself.
sushi.6: Write being too tired to go on, then one thought clears it and it is set down.
sushi.7: Admit most fine things aren't yours, and prize the free ones anyone may enjoy.
sushi.8: End without elevation, on one homely line teasing yourself.
sushi.9: Gently turn over a view everyone holds to give a deeper reading.
sushi.10: Neither believe nor dismiss hearsay; go and look first.
wangxiaobo.1: Take an absurd premise seriously and work it through like a math problem until the conclusion gives itself away.
wangxiaobo.2: Begin with a small thing "I" went through, as if talking to a friend.
wangxiaobo.3: Use common knowledge from physics, math, statistics or logic to compare social phenomena.
wangxiaobo.4: Write gravely of an animal's "choices" and "dignity" to reflect on people.
wangxiaobo.5: Treat "is it interesting, does it make you think" as a serious standard.
wangxiaobo.6: The narrator admits to being dim, lazy or timid before making the argument.
wangxiaobo.7: Join no loud side; just say clearly what you saw.
wangxiaobo.8: Lift slogans, officialese and big words intact and use them earnestly in trivial scenes.
wangxiaobo.9: Tell absurd things in an even, mild voice, without exclamation, and let readers laugh.
wangxiaobo.10: No elevation or rallying: follow the reasoning to a light conclusion or a self-joke.
wangzengqi.1: Don't state the theme; start casually from a place, a thing, or an idle remark.
wangzengqi.2: Like a knowing friend, say what a thing is called, its local names, how it's made and eaten.
wangzengqi.3: Get a craft's tools, steps, timing and jargon exactly right, without praise.
wangzengqi.4: One or two actions and one line, and the person stands.
wangzengqi.5: Wander to another place, year or thing, then return without a seam.
wangzengqi.6: Lay out a place's seasons, rules and households first; people and events grow out of them.
wangzengqi.7: Name the plants, give their look, smell, habitat and use, and don't make them carry feeling.
wangzengqi.8: Short sentences that read aloud; a long one is followed by a very short one.
wangzengqi.9: Slip in a familiar classical phrase or old name, no more than three times in a piece.
wangzengqi.10: No summing up: stop on a small matter, an idle remark, or an image.
yuhua.1: Tell the heaviest things in the calm voice of small talk or bookkeeping; the narrator never judges.
yuhua.2: The same act recurs at several points, changing a little each time.
yuhua.3: A death gets a sentence or two; the next sentence is an everyday action.
yuhua.4: At the heaviest point, place an absurd, funny detail that takes off half the weight.
yuhua.5: Short, plain lines go back and forth and move the story; the only tag is "said".
yuhua.6: Use sums of money, counts, weights and years instead of adjectives.
yuhua.7: An outsider "I" listens to someone tell their own life.
yuhua.8: One small object runs from start to end, carrying more feeling each time it appears.
yuhua.9: Characters make fun of themselves; the laugh is how they bear things.
yuhua.10: Return to an everyday image, a homely line, or an action, without elevation.
zhangailing.1: Open with a slightly arbitrary pronouncement, then prove it slowly with detail.
zhangailing.2: Compare an abstract feeling to something concrete, everyday and far-fetched.
zhangailing.3: Leave the feeling unsaid; show how someone handles an object.
zhangailing.4: One or two colors, fastidiously exact, set the emotional key.
zhangailing.5: Write out the calculations inside human ties calmly, like keeping books, without blame.
zhangailing.6: Write vegetable prices, power bills and frozen dumplings with relish, never disdain.
zhangailing.7: In a lively or trivial moment, add one stroke of time, leaving or loss, and it turns cold.
zhangailing.8: Change scene on a sound or a beam of light, marking a shift in time or mood.
zhangailing.9: Having seen through someone's small scheme, turn back with a line on their behalf.
zhangailing.10: End on a cold, light pronouncement, dropped in passing, never elevated.
sanlian.1: Say "everyone feels this way", then take it apart yourself.
sanlian.2: Use a current meme as a verb or modifier to set the tone of a phenomenon in one line.
sanlian.3: Put three concrete nouns side by side in place of one abstraction.
sanlian.4: Describe small daily things earnestly in the language of markets, armies or offices.
sanlian.5: In about thirty characters, a scene with a person, a line and a turn.
sanlian.6: Compress a group into one label and give it a personality, like a single person.
sanlian.7: Tag plus name plus role plus one line in their own words.
sanlian.8: Voice the reader's distaste first, then answer it clearly.
sanlian.9: Three rising steps, and the third turns up the laugh.
sanlian.10: End by reusing the opening keyword so it takes on another layer of meaning.
sanlian.11: Give an old phenomenon a new name; the naming is the argument.
sanlian.12: No slogans, no verdict: land back in a concrete scene of daily life.
sanlian.13: Take an online phrase as the topic: trace its source, who uses it, and the mindset behind it.
sanlian.14: Extend one meme into a set of same-shaped siblings, adding length and laughs.
sanlian.15: Write the point as a quotable line, on its own line, in bold.
sanlian.16: Four to eight characters, flat and final, ending in a full stop.
sanlian.17: Explain an everyday object or gesture with straight-faced technical terms.
sanlian.18: Drop in a popular science word (dopamine, cortisol) as seasoning, not evidence.
sanlian.19: Pair "it used to be... now..." or an old word with a new one to show how ideas changed.
sanlian.20: Close by pressing the point down to the plainest standard of everyday life.
sanlian.21: One word with two meanings, used as a headline-grade joke.
acheng.1: The first sentence is an event, a scene or a place, with no historical setup.
acheng.2: Write eating as a solemn series of actions: not whether it tastes good, only how it is eaten.
acheng.3: Don't write what people think or feel, only what their hands, eyes and bodies do.
acheng.4: A character enters with one line or one habit, stands, and is never explained.
acheng.5: Very short exchanges, mostly without "he said", revealing the measure between people.
acheng.6: Let an ordinary person state a plain truth in homely words; the narrator doesn't respond.
acheng.7: Vernacular words, but clipped classical rhythm, landing at paragraph ends.
acheng.8: The heaviest event gets the fewest words, sometimes only a trace left after.
acheng.9: Set the most common thing beside something of the Way, and say neither is higher.
acheng.10: Stop on an ordinary action or line, without summary or sigh.
versailles.1: Tuck the noun being shown off into an adverbial or a clause; the main clause is about something small.
versailles.2: Complain about the "faults" of good things: too big, too many, too fast.
versailles.3: Say you're not good enough, by an absurdly high standard.
versailles.4: The praise comes from someone else; you only pass it on, helplessly.
versailles.5: Refer to brands, schools and places by abbreviation, color or nickname, like old friends.
versailles.6: Pair big numbers with deflating words: "only", "just", "barely", "under".
versailles.7: Present an advantage as a serious problem that needs solving.
versailles.8: End by asking readers for advice; the question itself is the boast.
versailles.9: Treat ordinary people's daily life as a novelty, pretending not to know the going rates.
versailles.10: End on a sigh or a tired face, never saying it outright.
feature.1: Open on one concrete image or moment, putting the reader on the scene.
feature.2: Set a literary quotation before the text to fix the tone, then turn to the subject.
feature.3: Hand feeling and information to the subject's direct quotes; key quotes are short, spoken, physical.
feature.4: Objects, weather and work gestures are written into the person's situation, each with a source.
feature.5: Fit decades of a life into one paragraph, at the pace of a CV.
feature.6: Open by asserting something unusual or improbable about the person, creating tension.
feature.7: For a group story, one person, one scene, one life per section; individuals add up to the event's weight.
feature.8: Pain and emotion come only from the pressure of facts, without one lyrical word.
feature.9: Use nouns or figurative phrases as subheads: restrained, poetic, no spoilers.
feature.10: Investigative features end with a reading list; the text relays research through detail, not jargon.
gongwen.1: Before drafting, ask two or three questions to fill in issuer, recipient, matter, date, classification and urgency.
gongwen.2: Pick the document type by the reporting relationship, and explain why.
gongwen.3: Read all the user's material, extract facts, figures and usable wording, and summarize before drafting.
gongwen.4: Respectful upward, clear downward, consultative between peers.
gongwen.5: Urgent matters brief and to the point; major matters full and thorough.
gongwen.6: Title, recipient, body, signature and record block all present, with correct numbering of levels.
gongwen.7: Read the draft through silently, fix the awkward, cut the wordy, then check the common-errors list.
gongwen.8: When handing over, explain the tone chosen and what can be adjusted.
gongwen.9: With the user's consent, record observed preferences in a style profile and apply them next time.
